title: Prophylactic immunity that prevents the common non-viral cancers

concept.text: The proposed innovation is immunization given before a person develops diagnosed cancer or a known precancer, creating durable immune surveillance that prevents common non-viral cancers from becoming established. Its ambitious scope is protection against most lung, colorectal, breast, prostate and pancreatic cancers. The intended benefit is fewer first cancers among vaccinated people, rather than reduced recurrence after treatment.

Conceptual synthesis: this capability would require immune protection that recognizes and eliminates dangerous emerging lesions while preserving healthy tissues. It need not depend on one vaccine formulation or one antigen shared by all cancers. A historical, stricter variant proposes a short vaccination course against one conserved antigen present in every malignancy, followed by lifelong, complete protection. That variant remains a proposed mechanism within the broader capability; neither the existence of the required antigen nor lifelong protection is established by the supplied evidence.

Two existing precedents help explain the goal. HPV vaccination demonstrates cancer prevention through protection against a cancer-causing infection. Individualized melanoma vaccination demonstrates immune targeting based on mutations identified in an existing tumor. Neither precedent establishes durable primary prevention of the common non-viral cancers in people without diagnosed cancer or known precancer.

significance.text: If safe immunization prevented most cases across the five named cancer sites for many years, a substantial fall in their incidence among vaccinated people would follow directly. Like vaccination against serious infections, it would move protection to a period when recipients are still healthy. The analogy concerns prevention before disease: it does not establish that cancer offers an equally predictable target or that infection-blocking vaccine mechanisms transfer to non-viral cancers.

The scale of cancer burden makes that possibility consequential. Cancer statistics, 2025 reports US lifetime probabilities of an invasive cancer diagnosis of 39.9% for men and 39.0% for women. Table 3 uses 2018–2021 data excluding 2020, and excludes basal and squamous cell skin cancers and in situ carcinoma except urinary bladder. These are dated, all-site population estimates, not the proportion preventable by this proposed immunization. They also do not imply that cancer is inevitable with aging.

Conditional downstream possibilities include fewer cancer operations and courses of systemic treatment, less treatment-related disability, and lower demands on cancer services. Those effects would depend on which cancers are prevented, the duration and distribution of protection, uptake, harms and practical delivery. Reduced incidence alone would not quantify mortality reduction or establish a favorable overall balance of benefits and harms.

The scope matters. Prevention of two cancer types over several years would be an important initial demonstration, but would not establish prevention of most cases across all five named sites, protection against every malignancy, or lifelong immunity. Protection against future cancers would also leave treatment of established tumors and management of known precancers as separate clinical needs; it would not itself demonstrate either capability.

missing_breakthrough.text: The proposed missing capability is durable, safe immune recognition of lesions on the path to common non-viral cancers before a diagnosed tumor or known precancer supplies a treatment target. Its central design requirement is selective protection: emerging dangerous cells would have to be controlled without widespread injury to normal tissue or unacceptable autoimmune disease. This is a statement of the capability sought and its safety requirement. The retained evidence does not establish the precise biological obstacles or prove that the capability remains absent as of November 1, 2026.

A concrete targeting problem follows from the difference between prospective prevention and individualized treatment. The supplied melanoma report describes an approach using tumor and normal DNA from an individual patient to identify mutations unique to that patient's cancer. A preventive approach for someone without a diagnosed tumor would need a way to select effective targets without relying on that same existing-tumor workflow. The report illustrates this difference, but does not prove that future tumor targets cannot be anticipated.

Engineering synthesis: unresolved requirements include selecting targets with sufficient coverage across the intended cancers and recipients, sustaining effective immune protection for years, maintaining discrimination from healthy tissue, and determining whether boosters or multiple formulations are needed. The supplied evidence does not resolve whether a shared-target strategy, individualized risk-based strategy, or another approach could meet these requirements. It also does not substantiate a blanket assertion that all shared cancer antigens are self proteins.

The universal-antigen variant adds separate demands: establishing that the target occurs in every malignancy, that targeting it safely prevents disease, and that a short course produces lifelong protection. Those premises and their comparative feasibility remain unestablished. The broader concept should therefore remain open to multiple mechanisms rather than depending on this stricter variant.

current_state.text: Cancer statistics, 2025 provides a documented infection-related prevention precedent. It describes the potential for HPV vaccination to virtually eliminate cervical cancer and reports a 69% decline in cervical cancer incidence rates among women aged 20–24 years, a group first exposed to HPV vaccination. This supports the relevance of vaccination to cancer prevention. It does not establish prevention of common non-viral cancers, prevention of every virus-caused cancer, or the approval status of non-viral preventive vaccines.

An October 23, 2026 Dermatology Times report describes improved recurrence-free and distant metastasis-free survival with individualized neoantigen therapy plus pembrolizumab compared with pembrolizumab alone after complete melanoma resection. The intervention addresses patients who have already had cancer. It therefore supplies a postoperative immune-treatment precedent, not evidence of preventing first cancers in healthy people. The reported comparison concerns combination treatment and does not establish vaccine-alone efficacy.

The same article describes a phase 3 trial enrolling 1,137 patients with completely resected stage IIB–IV melanoma. That enrollment figure describes a postoperative trial population; it is not a healthy-person prevention cohort or an efficacy estimate. The supplied review had the full news article, but its referenced primary trial publication and registry were not supplied for independent inspection. The result should consequently retain its attribution to the dated secondary report, without inferring unprovided effect sizes or treating the enrollment figure as evidence of preventive efficacy.

The research attributes a statement about the absence of approved non-infection-blocking cancer prevention vaccines to a Domchek and Vonderheide article in Cancer Discovery, April 2024, volume 14, pages 600–604. No artifact of the intended PDF was captured, so the supplied review could not verify that statement, its wording or its scope. It cannot support a definitive conclusion about the approval landscape in November 2026. Missing access is an evidence limitation, not evidence that the attributed statement is false.

The retained Cancer statistics, 2025 XML was partial and truncated within the references, although the supplied review located the relevant statistics and HPV passages in its body and tables. The supplied freshness record contains no bounded search evidence about subsequent preventive advances. Taken together, these materials establish relevant prevention and postoperative-treatment precedents, but establish neither achievement of the full ONC-09 capability nor its definitive absence as of November 1, 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed initial demonstration: a randomized trial in people without diagnosed cancer or known precancer shows a large reduction in first-cancer incidence for at least two common non-viral cancers, sustained over several years, with autoimmune disease remaining uncommon. This is a proposed milestone, not an established consensus standard. The effect size, follow-up duration, eligible population and acceptable frequency and severity of harms would need prespecified definitions.
completion_criteria.label: Large, sustained first-cancer reductions across two common non-viral cancers

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evidentiary requirements: the trial should measure cancer incidence directly, with consistent ascertainment across groups, rather than relying only on an immune response as a substitute for prevention. Follow-up should establish how protection changes over time and capture delayed harms. Independent replication and evidence across relevant recipient groups would strengthen confidence in reproducibility and clarify where the benefit applies.
completion_criteria.label: Direct cancer-incidence measurement tracks protection duration and delayed harms

completion_criteria.text: Proposed broader demonstration: extending the claim to prevention of most lung, colorectal, breast, prostate and pancreatic cancers would require persuasive evidence for each named site, with adequate precision about the fraction prevented and duration of protection. Results should define practical boundaries such as age at vaccination, baseline risk, dosing, booster needs and populations studied. Finite trials establish demonstrated breadth and duration; they cannot establish literal universality or lifelong protection beyond observed follow-up.
completion_criteria.label: Prevention of most cancers demonstrated at each named site

completion_criteria.text: The endpoint must remain distinct from postoperative relapse prevention. A trial showing fewer recurrences after complete melanoma resection can support a therapeutic claim, but cannot satisfy a proposed demonstration of fewer first cancers among people without diagnosed cancer or known precancer.
completion_criteria.label: Fewer first cancers demonstrated in cancer-free people without known precancer

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: ONC-08, Interception of non-viral precancers before they invade, is the closest neighboring capability. ONC-09 proposes immunization before a known precancer is present, whereas ONC-08 explicitly concerns interception of precancer. A successful ONC-09 mechanism might act on microscopic emerging lesions, creating biological overlap, but its intended recipient population and preventive demonstration remain distinct.

Roster-based synthesis: ONC-02, Sterilizing immune clearance of established metastatic carcinomas, concerns eliminating existing advanced disease. ONC-03, Eradication of dormant disseminated tumor cells that cause late relapse, concerns cells left after a cancer has already developed. Both may share immune mechanisms with ONC-09, but first-cancer prevention does not establish either therapeutic capability. The postoperative melanoma report is relevant to treatment and recurrence, without by itself proving eradication of dormant disseminated cells.

Roster-based synthesis: ONC-01, Mortality-reducing detection of lethal cancers while they are still localized, and ONC-10, A reliable distinction between early neoplasms that will kill and those that will not, concern finding and interpreting disease. They could complement prevention by identifying cancers that arise despite vaccination or clarifying which early lesions matter. Detection, risk classification and reduced incidence remain different achievements.

Roster-based synthesis: ONC-04, A shared malignant dependency that renewing normal tissues can spare, overlaps with the search for selective vulnerabilities, but a malignant dependency is not necessarily a usable immune antigen. ONC-05, Therapies that drive the whole clonal population to extinction, concerns eliminating an existing cancer population. ONC-06, Stable reversion of carcinoma cells to non-malignant tissue identity, changes cell state. These are distinct mechanisms and endpoints from prospective immunization.

Roster-based synthesis: ONC-07, Body-wide delivery that alters essentially every malignant cell, and ONC-12, Off-the-shelf cell therapy that matches autologous cures and can be given at ordinary scale, address delivery or treatment-platform capabilities that could inform some preventive strategies. Neither is established as a prerequisite for ONC-09. ONC-11, Real-time, cell-resolution guidance that makes incomplete cancer surgery uncommon, addresses surgical completeness after disease exists and remains relevant to cancers not prevented. These relationships are inferred from the supplied roster titles; full specifications of the other concepts were not supplied.

change_log.reason: The concept remains coherent even where supporting assertions or current-status claims require qualification.

change_log.change: Integrated infection-blocking prevention and postoperative individualized vaccination as separate precedents.
change_log.reason: Both explain relevant progress, but neither demonstrates primary prevention of common non-viral cancers.

change_log.change: Corrected the interpretation and provenance of the 39.9% and 39.0% lifetime cancer probabilities.
change_log.reason: The supplied review located them in the body and Table 3, with specific data years and exclusions; they are not vaccine-preventable fractions or evidence that cancer is inevitable.

change_log.change: Removed the unverifiable Domchek and Vonderheide quotation and qualified the claimed November 2026 approval gap.
change_log.reason: The intended PDF was not captured, and the empty freshness record does not establish the contemporary approval landscape.

change_log.change: Added the melanoma report's date, combination-treatment scope, postoperative population and 1,137-patient phase 3 enrollment detail with appropriate limits.
change_log.reason: These details clarify what was reported without implying vaccine-alone efficacy or prevention in healthy recipients.

change_log.change: Retained the universal-antigen variant while qualifying its biological premises and comparative feasibility.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence does not establish a universal antigen, blanket claims about shared antigens, or the impossibility of anticipating future tumor targets.

change_log.change: Separated a proposed two-cancer milestone from the broader five-site ambition and added operational and reproducibility requirements.
change_log.reason: Initial success would demonstrate bounded protection, not universal, lifelong or five-site efficacy.

change_log.change: Used the supplied roster to explain relationships with the other oncology concepts.
change_log.reason: Roster titles permit bounded comparisons even though full specifications are unavailable; no entries need to be merged or removed.

unresolved_issues: Whether any qualifying non-viral primary-prevention vaccine was approved or demonstrated by November 1, 2026 remains unresolved in the supplied evidence.
The attributed 2024 Domchek and Vonderheide statement, its context and its scope remain unverified because the intended PDF artifact was not captured.
The primary melanoma trial publication and registry were not supplied; the reported treatment findings cannot be independently assessed beyond the supplied secondary-source review.
The antigen strategy, attainable coverage, duration of protection and autoimmune risk for the proposed capability remain unresolved.
The existence and safety of a target shared by every malignancy, and the comparative feasibility of the stricter universal-antigen variant, remain unestablished.
Effect size, follow-up, acceptable harms and population boundaries for the proposed demonstrations still require prespecified definitions.
Relationships with other oncology concepts remain limited to their supplied roster titles rather than full specifications.

brief.title: Vaccines that prevent common cancers
possible: Healthy people could get vaccinated to prevent most lung, colorectal, breast, prostate and pancreatic cancers unrelated to viruses. Their immune system would recognize dangerous emerging cells and remove them before cancer takes hold. Protection would begin before any cancer or precancer—a change that can lead to cancer—is diagnosed.
why: Fewer people would face a first cancer diagnosis. Preventing these cancers could also mean fewer operations, fewer courses of cancer drugs and less treatment-related disability, while reducing pressure on cancer services.

sources.showed: They reported that a personalized vaccine combined with pembrolizumab, an immune treatment, reduced recurrence or death after surgery for melanoma, a skin cancer, compared with pembrolizumab alone.
sources.quote: the combination reduced the risk of recurrence or death by 42% compared with pembrolizumab alone
sources.cited_for: Personalized vaccination can help target cancer after surgery.
sources.not_established: This does not establish vaccine-alone protection or prevention of first cancers in healthy people.

sources.showed: This is an article discussing the approval status of cancer prevention vaccines that do not work by blocking infections.
sources.cited_for: It addresses the distinction between infection-blocking vaccines and other cancer prevention vaccines.
sources.not_established: An approval-status discussion does not demonstrate safe, lasting prevention of common cancers unrelated to viruses.

sources.who: Rebecca L. Siegel and colleagues, American Cancer Society
sources.showed: They documented cancer trends and a decline in cervical cancer among young women first exposed to vaccination against HPV, a cancer-causing virus.
sources.quote: Overall cancer incidence has generally declined in men but has risen in women
sources.cited_for: Cancer remains a substantial burden, and vaccination against a cancer-causing infection provides a prevention precedent.
sources.not_established: Preventing infection-related cancer does not establish prevention of cancers unrelated to viruses.

shown: Vaccination against HPV already provides a cancer prevention precedent. Merck and Moderna also reported fewer recurrences or deaths with a personalized vaccine plus immune treatment after melanoma surgery. That vaccine uses mutations from an existing tumor to choose its targets.
missing: A way to choose effective immune targets before a person has a diagnosed tumor or known precancer.
Protection lasting for years that removes dangerous cells while sparing healthy tissue and avoiding serious immune attacks on the body.
Direct evidence of preventing most cancers at every intended site, with clear dosing and booster needs.

milestones.label: Sustained prevention across at least two common cancers
milestones.explanation: A randomized trial in people without cancer or known precancer would have to show large first-cancer reductions lasting years, with immune attacks on the body uncommon. This would establish an initial prevention benefit.

milestones.label: Cancer tracking reveals protection duration and delayed harms
milestones.explanation: Follow-up would have to count cancers consistently across groups and track fading protection and delayed harms. Independent replication across relevant groups would strengthen confidence beyond an immune response alone.

milestones.label: Most cancers prevented at every intended site
milestones.explanation: Evidence would have to establish prevention of most lung, colorectal, breast, prostate and pancreatic cancers, with duration and dosing boundaries defined. This would establish the intended breadth of protection.

milestones.label: Fewer first cancers in people without known precancer
milestones.explanation: A trial would have to demonstrate fewer first cancers in people without diagnosed cancer or known precancer. Preventing recurrence after cancer surgery cannot establish this benefit.

uncertain: It remains unclear which targets could cover the intended cancers safely and how long protection could last.
A safe target shared by every cancer, and lifelong protection from a short vaccination course, remain unestablished.
The required benefit, follow-up duration and acceptable harms still need clear definitions.

page.title: Primary prevention vaccines for non-viral cancers
page.definition: A vaccine would reduce the risk of a first invasive cancer by training the immune system to recognize emerging abnormal cells in people with no history of cancer and no known precancer. Its targets could include neoantigens, protein fragments altered by mutations in those cells. The approved HPV and hepatitis B vaccines act earlier by preventing a cancer-causing infection. Lung, colorectal, breast, prostate and pancreatic cancers are assessed separately.

goal.need: People with Lynch syndrome undergo colonoscopy to find and remove precancerous growths. Among 1,942 carriers with no previous cancer, 151 developed colorectal cancer during 13,782 person-years of surveillance. A vaccine could help the immune system recognize abnormal cells before a growth is detectable, sparing some people an invasive cancer and its treatment. The benefit depends on the emerging cells carrying the vaccine target and on the immune response sparing healthy tissue.

completion.title: FDA licenses a vaccine for primary prevention of a non-viral cancer.
completion.criterion: For a cancer site, FDA grants a biologics licence with an indication to prevent first invasive cancers in a specified population without diagnosed cancer or known precancer. The product and manufacturing facilities meet applicable safety, purity and potency requirements. Achievement is indication-specific: one site's licence does not establish the other cases, protection against most cases, or lifelong immunity.
completion.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 601.2(a) and (d); the licensing test is applied separately to each cancer site.
completion.threshold_quote: data derived from nonclinical laboratory and clinical studies which demonstrate that the manufactured product meets prescribed requirements of safety, purity, and potency
completion.basis: FDA weighs benefits and risks for the intended population and the disease to be prevented. The approved prescribing information identifies the indication and population supported by the evidence. The US cancer-prevention vaccines for HPV and hepatitis B protect against infection.

milestones.title: A preventive cancer vaccine shows preliminary efficacy in a relevant animal model.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate preliminary preventive efficacy in an animal model relevant to the specified cancer. The experiment must measure a tumour outcome, such as incidence, multiplicity or burden, after preventive vaccination. PREVENT sets no common minimum effect size.
milestones.set_by: National Cancer Institute, PREVENT Cancer Preclinical Drug Development Program, minimal entry criteria.
milestones.threshold_quote: Preliminary efficacy in relevant animal models

milestones.title: A participant receives a preventive cancer vaccine under an effective investigational new drug application.
milestones.criterion: Document administration of the vaccine to at least one participant with no history of cancer and no known precancer in the prevention cohort for the specified site. The investigational new drug application must be in effect: ordinarily 30 days after FDA receives it without imposing a clinical hold, or on earlier FDA notification that the investigation may begin.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 312.40.
milestones.threshold_quote: An investigator may not administer an investigational new drug to human subjects until the IND goes into effect under paragraph (b) of this section.

milestones.title: A preventive cancer vaccine has human safety and pharmacology data sufficient for phase 2.
milestones.criterion: Obtain human safety and pharmacology data sufficient to design a controlled phase 2 study for primary prevention at the specified site. For a study that also enrols cancer survivors or people with known precancer, identify the evidence applicable to the primary-prevention population. Assess any immune-response endpoint using the study's own definition.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 312.21(a). Numerical immune-response criteria remain specific to each study.
milestones.threshold_quote: permit the design of well-controlled, scientifically valid, Phase 2 studies.

milestones.title: A controlled prevention trial yields preliminary evidence that a cancer vaccine is effective.
milestones.criterion: A controlled prevention trial provides preliminary evidence of effectiveness on its prespecified efficacy endpoint in the population studied. Apply the protocol's endpoint definition, comparison and follow-up. If the endpoint combines invasive cancer with precancerous lesions, a reduction in the composite supports a claim about that combined outcome. A claim of fewer first invasive cancers requires evidence specific to invasive cancer.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 312.21(b)–(c). TRIAD5-Plus illustrates a colorectal protocol, not a threshold for other cancer sites.
milestones.threshold_quote: after preliminary evidence suggesting effectiveness of the drug has been obtained

milestones.title: Pivotal studies establish a preventive cancer vaccine's effectiveness and benefit–risk for labeling.
milestones.criterion: Adequate, well-controlled clinical evidence establishes effectiveness for the proposed primary-prevention indication, with safety information sufficient to evaluate benefit–risk and support labeling. For this entry's indication, recipients begin without diagnosed cancer or known precancer and the claim concerns first invasive cancers. Effect size, statistical boundary and follow-up are those accepted for the indication; these regulations specify no universal numerical threshold.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 312.21(c) and 314.126, applied to the proposed primary-prevention indication.
milestones.threshold_quote: Reports of adequate and well-controlled investigations provide the primary basis for determining whether there is “substantial evidence”

milestones.title: The vaccine completes the preclinical safety studies needed for first human dosing.
milestones.criterion: Complete the studies needed to support an investigational new drug application for the proposed vaccine. As appropriate to the candidate, these include dose-range or maximum-tolerated-dose studies in relevant species and toxicology and pharmacology studies conducted under good laboratory practice.
milestones.set_by: National Cancer Institute, Development of Cancer Immunoprevention Agents, Phase II project activities
milestones.threshold_quote: Perform IND-enabling studies as appropriate for the agent under development:

milestones.title: FDA accepts a biologics licence application for the cancer-prevention indication for filing.
milestones.criterion: FDA accepts the biologics licence application for filing after receiving the pertinent information and data for the product. The application seeks an indication to prevent a first invasive cancer at the specified site in the intended population.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, 21 CFR 601.2(a)
milestones.threshold_quote: shall not be considered as filed until all pertinent information and data have been received by the Food and Drug Administration.

not_found: No external criterion requiring prevention of most cases across all five sites, or lifelong protection, was found in the NCI programmes, FDA regulations and prevention protocols searched.
No published randomised result demonstrating fewer first invasive cancers in recipients without previous cancer or known precancer was located for the five cases.
No human primary-prevention vaccine result was located for prostate cancer.
No position rejecting primary-prevention vaccination as infeasible or unworthy of pursuit was found in the NCI, AACR or Cancer Research UK materials searched.

results.finding: The KRAS multipeptide vaccine reduced surface lung tumour multiplicity by about 86% in 17 mice.
No toxicity was observed with the KRAS multipeptide vaccine in the efficacy experiment (9 vaccinated mice).
results.detail: The report provides no dose-ranging or maximum-tolerated-dose results and documents no toxicology or pharmacology studies conducted under good laboratory practice.
results.quote: Meanwhile, no toxicity was observed in targeting wild-type KRAS.

results.finding: Preventively vaccinated Lynch syndrome mice had 34.2% lower mean intestinal tumor burden (19 vaccinated, 11 controls).
results.detail: Sample sizes are from the tumor-burden analysis in Table 2. The endpoint summed tumor weights across intestinal sites, and tumors in this model occur predominantly in the small intestine.

recurrent FSP neoantigen vaccination
reduced tumor burden (mean control, 71.84 mg vs vacci-

results.finding: Lalba-M in NMU-challenged rats (12 per arm in Study 7) increased the share free of both palpable tumors and micro-DCIS by 25 percentage points.
results.detail: Study 7 combines two outcomes. In Study 5, palpable tumors occurred in 10 of 12 rats in each arm.
results.quote: In Study 7, neither palpable tumors nor micro-DCIS were detected in 9 out of 12 rats in the Lalba-M group, compared to 6 out of 12 in the Luc group

results.finding: All Lalba-U rats developed injection-site scars in the short-term safety studies (group size unstated).
results.detail: The studies used a fixed dose. The authors identify longer-term safety and effects during pregnancy and lactation as areas for further study.

results.finding: In Lobund–Wistar rats (30 per group), the whole-cell vaccine reduced de novo prostate tumor occurrence by 90% versus media-vaccinated controls.
results.quote: Groups of 30 GFT cell–vaccinated rats showed a 90% reduction, and PTE-vaccinated rats, a 50% reduction in the occurrence of de novo prostate tumors compared with media-vaccinated controls.

).

results.finding: In the MUC1 lung cancer prevention pilot, 49 of 50 registered participants received the initial injection.
results.detail: Eligibility excluded recent malignancy and allowed small CT nodules. The paper reports ethics approval and trial registration but gives no FDA IND status.
results.quote: All 49 participants received the week 0 vaccine injection

results.finding: Among 45 evaluable heavy smokers vaccinated with MUC1, 13.3% met the prespecified immune-response endpoint.
results.detail: The response rate was lower than anticipated. The authors identified unresolved questions about immunosuppression and participant selection.
results.quote:
There were 6 immune responders to the vaccine (4 of 27 current smokers (14.8%) and 2 
of 18 former smokers (11.1%) among the 45 evaluable participants for an overall response rate 
of 13.3% (95% confidence interval [CI] 5.1%, 26.8%).

results.finding: Under an FDA-authorized IND, 40 participants with prior advanced colorectal adenoma received the MUC1 vaccine.
results.detail: Of 46 participants who consented, six received no vaccine and one withdrew after the first injection, leaving 39 evaluable for immunogenicity.
results.quote: Of the 46 subjects who consented to participate, 6 did not receive vaccine: four had abnormal screening laboratory tests, one did not meet criteria for an advanced adenoma, and one declined to participate.

results.finding: Among 39 evaluable MUC1 vaccine recipients with prior advanced colorectal adenoma, 43.6% met the prespecified anti-MUC1 IgG response criterion.
results.quote: shows that week 12 IgG/prevaccination IgG ratio ≥ 2.0 was observed in 17/39 subjects (43.6%; range in ratio among responders: 2.2 to 36.3).

results.finding: Alpha-lactalbumin vaccination yielded 0 breast cancers in mice bred to develop the disease. Sample size was unreported.
results.quote:
Cleveland Clinic researchers have demonstrated in animal studies that vaccination against alpha -lactalbumin 
completely prevented breast cancer in mice that were specifically bred to develop breast cancer.

results.finding: Phase 1 Cohort Ib vaccinated all 4 women with no prior breast cancer or other cancer before prophylactic mastectomy.
results.detail: The filing describes prophylactic surgery but supplies no eligibility rule or baseline findings establishing that at least one of the four recipients had no known precancer.
results.quote:
Cohort Ib (n=4), cancer-free women with BRCA1, BRCA2, or PALB2 mutations who elected preventive mastectomy and were 
vaccinated prior to surgery

results.finding: The 35-participant Phase 1 breast vaccine trial reported a 74% protocol-defined immune response across the study.
results.detail: The filing describes a potential Phase 2 neoadjuvant combination study in newly diagnosed patients. The prevention cohort's protocol-defined response rate is unreported.
results.quote: protocol defined immune responses were observed in 74% of the study subjects

results.finding: Of 45 Lynch syndrome carriers vaccinated with Nous-209, 26 had no cancer history.
results.detail: The paper reports protocol and institutional review board approvals and trial registration. FDA IND status at first dosing is unspecified.
results.quote:
A total of 45 healthy LS participants enrolled between Novem -
ber 2022 and November 2023 were vaccinated (Fig. 1b)

results.finding: Among 37 evaluable Lynch syndrome carriers given Nous-209, 100% met the week 9 immune-response endpoint.
results.detail: ELISpot positivity required at least 50 spot-forming cells per million PBMCs and at least twice background. Response required reactivity to at least one peptide pool. With baseline reactivity, the protocol required at least an 80% increase in at least one pool.
results.quote:
Neoantigen-specific immune responses were 
observed after vaccination in 100% of evaluable participants (n = 37)

results.finding: Among 43 Nous-209 recipients with follow-up colonoscopy, zero had an advanced adenoma at about one year.
results.detail: The protocol scheduled cohort 1 endoscopy at week 52 ± 14 days. Advanced adenoma was defined by diameter greater than 10 mm, high-grade dysplasia or villous histology.
results.quote:
of the total 23 adenomas detected in 12 participants, none 
were classified as advanced adenomas (diameter > 10 mm, presence 
of high-grade dysplasia and/or villous histology), while two partici-
pants had advanced adenomas at baseline colonoscopy

results.finding: Four cancer-free women received the α-lactalbumin vaccine before preventive mastectomy.
results.quote:
Cohort Ib (n=4), cancer-free women with BRCA1, BRCA2, or PALB2 mutations who elected
preventive mastectomy and were vaccinated prior to surgery;

results.finding: In the Phase 1 α-lactalbumin breast vaccine trial (n=35), 74% had a protocol-defined immune response.
results.detail: The Phase 2 example described in the release is a neoadjuvant combination study in newly diagnosed breast cancer patients.
results.quote:
Final Phase 1 findings showed the investigational vaccine met all major primary endpoints,
was safe and well tolerated at the maximum tolerated dose (MTD), and elicited protocol-
defined immune responses in 74% of participants.

results.finding: mKRAS-VAX was administered to 20 high-risk participants, all with pancreatic IPMNs.
results.quote: From April 2022 to February 2026, we vaccinated 20 patients who met criteria for at least one of three high-risk cohorts defined based on familial and/or germline PDAC predisposition

results.finding: Of 20 high-risk mKRAS-VAX recipients with pancreatic IPMNs, 18 met the prespecified T-cell response threshold.
results.quote: Vaccination elicited a significant mKRAS-specific T cell response in 18/20 participants (90%).

results.finding: Among 16 MRI-evaluable mKRAS-VAX recipients, 37.5% had cyst reduction or resolution.
results.detail: All vaccinated participants had IPMNs at baseline. The authors note that imaging limitations could account for apparent resolution of some subcentimeter cysts.
results.quote: The vaccinated cohort demonstrated a higher rate of cyst reduction or resolution (37.5%) relative to the unvaccinated cohort (6.8%).

results.finding: MUC1 peptide vaccine was administered to 53 of 103 trial participants after advanced adenoma removal.
results.detail: Eligibility excluded prior colorectal cancer but allowed some histories of other malignancies.
results.quote: 53 participants received the MUC1 vaccine and 50 placebo.

results.finding: Among 102 evaluable participants, 25% of MUC1 vaccine recipients met the week-12 anti-MUC1 IgG response criterion.
results.quote: 13/52 (25%) of MUC1 vaccine recipients had a ≥2-fold increase in MUC1 IgG (range 2.9–17.3) at week 12 vs. 0/50 placebo recipients (1-sided Fisher’s exact P<0.0001).

results.finding: Among 95 participants with follow-up colonoscopy, the adjusted relative risk of adenoma recurrence with MUC1 vaccine versus placebo was 0.83.
results.detail: The prespecified analysis of participants who mounted an immune response after both initial vaccination and the booster also had a confidence interval that crossed 1. This subgroup was defined after vaccination.
results.quote: Recurrent adenoma was observed in 31 of 47 (66.0%) in the placebo group vs. 27 of 48 (56.3%) in the MUC1 group (adjusted relative risk (aRR) = 0.83 [95% CI, 0.60–1.14], P=0.25).

results.finding: In 19 KRAS-mutant mice, PAS vaccination was associated with a 23-percentage-point lower incidence of invasive pancreatic carcinoma at 8 months.
results.detail: Vaccination began at 3 months of age, when the mice already had low-grade PanIN. The result applies to vaccination during progression from established precursor lesions.
results.quote:
33.3% of control mice developed invasive carcinoma by month
8 and only 1 of the 10 PAS-treated mice developed cancer

results.finding: Four participants received the alpha-lactalbumin vaccine in the phase I breast cancer prevention cohort.
results.quote:
We vaccinated 26 
patients in Cohort Ia, 4 in Cohort Ib, and 5 in Cohort Ic.

results.finding: All 4 breast cancer prevention-cohort participants had Grade 1 injection-site reactions at dose level 1.
results.detail: The protocol defined response as ≥1 in 30,000 IFNγ- or IL-17-secreting T cells at day 56, or a threefold rise when baseline already met that threshold.

results.finding: All 20 Lynch syndrome safety-cohort participants completed the Tri-Ad5 prime and booster series.
results.quote: All 20 SP participants (median age 57.5 (range 42–75), 70% female, 15% minority) received all prime and booster series.

results.finding: Among 20 Lynch syndrome participants given Tri-Ad5 with or without NAI, zero treatment-related serious adverse events occurred.
results.detail: The protocol required both more than 250 qualifying antigen-specific T cells per million plated cells and a greater than twofold postvaccination increase to classify a participant as a responder. The paper reports no responder counts.
results.quote: AEs were predominantly grade 1; no treatment-related serious adverse events (SAEs) occurred.

results.finding: Prophylactic α-lactalbumin vaccination delayed mammary tumor growth in transgenic mice. Sample size and effect magnitude were unreported.
results.quote: Figure 2: α-lactalbumin vaccination delays and treats breast tumor growth.

results.finding: Anixa reported FDA clearance of the alpha-lactalbumin breast cancer vaccine IND by December 21, 2020 (preclinical sample size unreported).
results.detail: Completion is inferred from the FDA clearance reported in the company press release.
results.quote:
the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has cleared
the Investigational New Drug (IND) application for its breast cancer vaccine.

results.finding: In the α-lactalbumin breast vaccine prevention cohort (n=4), all participants had grade 1 injection-site reactions at dose level 1.
results.detail: The trial identified dose level 1 as the maximum tolerated dose. Prevention participants underwent risk-reducing mastectomy between days 57 and 84.

definition = "A vaccine would reduce the risk of a first invasive cancer by training the immune system to recognize emerging abnormal cells in people with no history of cancer and no known precancer. Its targets could include neoantigens, protein fragments altered by mutations in those cells. The approved HPV and hepatitis B vaccines act earlier by preventing a cancer-causing infection. Lung, colorectal, breast, prostate and pancreatic cancers are assessed separately.". Reason: The current definition reads as an established benefit and does not explain how the proposed vaccines differ from approved cancer-prevention vaccines.

goal.need = "People with Lynch syndrome undergo colonoscopy to find and remove precancerous growths. Among 1,942 carriers with no previous cancer, 151 developed colorectal cancer during 13,782 person-years of surveillance. A vaccine could help the immune system recognize abnormal cells before a growth is detectable, sparing some people an invasive cancer and its treatment. The benefit depends on the emerging cells carrying the vaccine target and on the immune response sparing healthy tissue.". Reason: The all-cancer lifetime figures do not show how much risk persists under current prevention or what a vaccine could add for people facing that risk.

add statement by Cancer Research UK and the CRIS Cancer Foundation, LungVax funding announcement, 2024: "to prevent lung cancer in people with a high risk of the disease.". Reason: The LungVax funding announcement identifies two funders that explicitly named primary prevention at one of the five cancer sites as a goal.

edit completion: basis = "FDA weighs benefits and risks for the intended population and the disease to be prevented. The approved prescribing information identifies the indication and population supported by the evidence. The US cancer-prevention vaccines for HPV and hepatitis B protect against infection.". Reason: The basis can identify where a reader can verify the licensed population and indication without repeating the search history.

edit m1: criterion = "Demonstrate preliminary preventive efficacy in an animal model relevant to the specified cancer. The experiment must measure a tumour outcome, such as incidence, multiplicity or burden, after preventive vaccination. PREVENT sets no common minimum effect size."; threshold_quote = "Preliminary efficacy in relevant animal models"; threshold_ref = 8; refs = [8, 2, 9, 22]. Reason: The animal experiment and prostate project listing obscure the PREVENT entry criterion and make it harder to apply consistently across sites.

add milestone after m1: "The vaccine completes the preclinical safety studies needed for first human dosing.". Reason: NCI identifies preclinical safety studies as a distinct step between preliminary animal efficacy and first human dosing.

edit m2: criterion = "Document administration of the vaccine to at least one participant with no history of cancer and no known precancer in the prevention cohort for the specified site. The investigational new drug application must be in effect: ordinarily 30 days after FDA receives it without imposing a clinical hold, or on earlier FDA notification that the investigation may begin."; threshold_quote = "An investigator may not administer an investigational new drug to human subjects until the IND goes into effect under paragraph (b) of this section."; threshold_ref = 12; refs = [12, 4, 35]. Reason: First dosing is the event that counts, and the published breast trial abstract distinguishes the four participants in the risk-reducing mastectomy cohort from the two treatment cohorts.

edit m3: criterion = "Obtain human safety and pharmacology data sufficient to design a controlled phase 2 study for primary prevention at the specified site. For a study that also enrols cancer survivors or people with known precancer, identify the evidence applicable to the primary-prevention population. Assess any immune-response endpoint using the study's own definition."; threshold_quote = "permit the design of well-controlled, scientifically valid, Phase 2 studies."; threshold_ref = 14. Reason: A pooled immune-response rate in cancer survivors and unaffected carriers, or a rate in people selected for pancreatic abnormalities, cannot by itself establish phase 2 readiness in the intended population.

edit m4: criterion = "A controlled prevention trial provides preliminary evidence of effectiveness on its prespecified efficacy endpoint in the population studied. Apply the protocol's endpoint definition, comparison and follow-up. If the endpoint combines invasive cancer with precancerous lesions, a reduction in the composite supports a claim about that combined outcome. A claim of fewer first invasive cancers requires evidence specific to invasive cancer."; threshold_quote = "after preliminary evidence suggesting effectiveness of the drug has been obtained"; threshold_ref = 14. Reason: The current criterion mixes an ongoing trial's enrolment with its efficacy test and leaves unclear what a change in the composite endpoint would establish.

add milestone after m5: "FDA accepts a biologics licence application for the cancer-prevention indication for filing.". Reason: FDA filing marks a verifiable regulatory step between obtaining pivotal evidence and receiving a licence.
remove not found 3. Reason: The Domchek–Vonderheide paper and the investigators' 2026 breast vaccine abstract are both available in full at the cited links.

add not found: "No position rejecting primary-prevention vaccination as infeasible or unworthy of pursuit was found in the NCI, AACR or Cancer Research UK materials searched.". Reason: Technical concerns about safety and target selection do not establish institutional opposition to pursuing the goal.
